---
title: "Web interface"
---

`onthesignal web` opens the whole of onthesignal in a browser: the signals of the session,
every analysis with interactive µPlot charts and its results under the chart, comparisons of
results, batches, SeedLink acquisition and real-time dashboard, a Python terminal working on
the signals, a code editor (Monaco) and the AI chat. It uses the same computations, commands,
scripts and configuration as the console, which remains available unchanged (`onthesignal`).

## Starting

```bash
pip install -e ".[web]"              # once: NiceGUI 4 and Jedi
onthesignal web                      # project = current folder, http://127.0.0.1:8080
onthesignal web data/*.mseed         # with files loaded at start-up
onthesignal web --project ~/bench3 --port 8090 --no-browser
```

The browser opens on `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. Ctrl+C in the shell stops the server; an
acquisition in progress is stopped cleanly and its data are saved.

The browser must be recent: Firefox, Chrome or Edge 121 or later, Safari 17.2 or later (the
minimum of NiceGUI 4). Every library is served by the server itself, so the interface works
without Internet access, except for SeedLink and the online AI providers.

One server serves one user, one project and one session. Several browser tabs can be open on
it: they share the session and stay synchronized. Reloading the page loses nothing — the
session, the Python terminal and the background jobs (acquisition, real time, batches,
reports) live in the server.

### As an application

The interface can be installed as an application, with its own window and an icon in the
menu of applications:

- **Chrome, Edge**: the install icon at the right of the address bar, or menu → *Cast, save
  and share* → *Install page as app…*; **Safari** (macOS): *File* → *Add to Dock*. Firefox
  does not install web applications.
- The installed application opens `http://127.0.0.1:8080` (the port used when installing it):
  the server must be running. If it is not, the window explains how to start it.
- **`onthesignal desktop`** goes further, like an Electron application: it starts the server
  itself on a free port and shows the interface in a window with its own web engine (Qt
  WebEngine, `pip install -e ".[desktop]"`); closing the window stops the server. The
  AppImage does the same without any installation ([Installation](installation.qmd#appimage)).

Browsers only install an application from `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` (an SSH tunnel is fine) or
HTTPS (`[web] tls_cert`, `tls_key`).

### Working from another computer

The server listens on the local machine only and has **no authentication**: anyone who can
reach its port can run Python code with your account. To work from a laptop, use an SSH
tunnel, which keeps the server local and protected by SSH:

```bash
ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 user@bench-pc
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8080 on the laptop
```

`--host 0.0.0.0` makes the server listen on the network; it prints a warning at start-up. Only
do this on a trusted network, ideally with `[web] code_execution = false`.

## Layout

```text
┌ header: project · search (/) · AI model · theme, terminal and chat buttons ──────────────┐
│ activity │ OBJECTS          │ work area: one tab per signal, result,   │ AI CHAT          │
│ bar      │ signals, results,│ file… — the chart on top, its results     │                  │
│          │ figures,variables│ below                                     │                  │
│          │ ── active view ──│──────────────────────────────────────────│                  │
│          │ Files, Analyses, │ PYTHON · OUTPUT · PROBLEMS · JOBS · HISTORY│                  │
│          │ Acquisition,     │                                           │                  │
│          │ Real time…       │                                           │                  │
└ status bar: signals and results, running jobs, AI model, UTC time ─────────────────────────┘
```

| Shortcut | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `/`, Ctrl+K | command palette: commands, signals, results, files |
| Ctrl+P | open a file or an object |
| Ctrl+Enter | run the open form |
| Ctrl+S | save the file in the editor |
| F5 | run the script open in the editor |
| Shift+Enter | run the selection (or the `# %%` cell) of the editor in the terminal |
| Ctrl+` | show or hide the Python terminal |
| Ctrl+Shift+I | show or hide the AI chat |
| Drag | zoom on the rectangle drawn (*Zoom* mode; a flat drag zooms the abscissa only), or move the chart (*Move* mode) |
| Middle button drag, Shift + mouse wheel | move along the abscissa of a chart |
| Ctrl + mouse wheel | zoom a chart in or out around the cursor |
| Shift+drag | select a time window on a plot |
| Double-click | back to the full view of a chart |

The palette also runs complete commands, as in the console: `/noise S1 fmax=50` runs the
analysis, `/noise` alone opens its form.

The theme button of the header (or the palette, *Toggle dark mode*) chooses a light or dark
theme, or that of the system (the default, `[web] theme`). The dark theme has its own colors
for the charts, validated on a dark background (contrast, color-vision deficiencies); the
editor and the terminal follow it.

### Navigating in a chart

Every chart has a toolbar at its top right, as the matplotlib windows:

| Button | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Home | full view (also a double-click on the chart) |
| ← / → | previous view / next view: every zoom or move can be undone and redone |
| Zoom (magnifier) | default mode: drag a rectangle to zoom in on it, as the *Zoom to rectangle* button of matplotlib; a drag flatter than about 30 pixels zooms the abscissa only |
| Move (four arrows) | drag the chart to move it, as the *Pan* button of matplotlib |

Whatever the mode, the middle button drags the chart, Shift + mouse wheel (or a horizontal
swipe of a touchpad) moves along the abscissa, and Ctrl + mouse wheel zooms around the cursor;
a plain wheel scrolls the page. The ordinate follows the visible data until a rectangle zoom
sets it; it then stays (and moves with a vertical drag in *Move* mode) until the full view.
The panels of a figure that share their abscissa (stacked signals, spectrogram and its time
series) zoom and move together along it; each keeps its own ordinate.

## Objects panel

The panel at the top left lists every object of the session; **one click displays it**:

| Group | Click |
| --- | --- |
| Signals (`S1`, `S2`…) | time plot, with the statistics of the visible window and the properties below |
| Results (`R1`, `R2`…) | the chart of the analysis and its results below |
| Figures | matplotlib figures shown by the terminal or a script |
| Variables | other variables of the Python terminal: numbers, arrays (plotted, or as a table for 2-D arrays), lists and dictionaries (as a tree)… |

Right-click opens the actions (rename, analyze, export, compare, add to report, ask the AI,
delete). The check boxes (or Ctrl+click) select several objects: a bar then offers *Overlay*
(the checked signals in one panel), *Stack* (one panel per signal, common time axis) and
*Compare* (results of the same analysis). An object can be dragged onto a time plot (the
signal is added to it), into the chat or into the editor. Results get stable session names
(`R1`, `R2`…) usable in the terminal (`R3["rms"]`); a terminal variable pointing to a result is
shown as an alias (`R3 · r`).

## Signals

- **Loading.** In the *Files* view, click a miniSEED file (or right-click → *Load with
  options…*); text files open an import assistant showing the first lines, where you give the
  number of channels, the time column and the sampling rate. Files can also be uploaded from
  the computer of the browser (*Upload*, or drag and drop): they are saved in `data/uploads/`
  of the project.
- **Plot.** The time plot uses relative seconds from the UTC instant written under the axis;
  the legend shows the absolute UTC time under the cursor. Zoom with the mouse: the visible
  window is reloaded at full resolution (an isolated spike of one sample always stays
  visible), with one window width on each side so that it can be moved at once. When a signal
  exceeds half of its full scale, the levels ±full scale/2 are drawn as red dashed lines. The table below gives the mean, standard deviation, peak-to-peak, minimum and
  maximum of the visible window. Each signal keeps its color in every plot of several
  signals and in the comparisons (`S1` blue, `S2` orange…).
- **Several signals.** *Overlay* or *Stack* in the objects panel, *Add signal* above a plot,
  or a signal dragged from the objects panel onto the plot. The chips above the plot remove a
  signal; *Overlay* / *Stacked* switches the display. Each signal keeps its color; signals in
  different units are overlaid with a warning (compare them in counts, or stack them).
- **Changing the samples.** In the terminal, `S4.data = S4.data + 100` shifts `S4` by 100
  counts (and `S4.data[:100] = 0` changes samples in place): the change is noted in the
  history of the signal (`samples modified`) and every plot of `S4` is redrawn. `S5 = S4 + 100`
  creates a shifted copy instead.
- **Selection.** Shift+drag selects a window: *Analyze selection…* opens an analysis with
  `t_start` and `t_end` filled in; *Slice to new signal* creates a new signal.
- **Properties.** Name, title, NSLC codes, unit, sensitivity (an expression such as
  `40 / 2**24` is accepted; `physical = counts × sensitivity`) and full scale are edited under
  the plot.
- **Test signals.** The `+` button of the panel creates test sines and noises of an ideal
  N-bit digitizer ([Test signals](test-signals.qmd)).

## Analyses and results

The *Analyses* view lists every analysis by category. A click opens a form generated from the
parameters of the analysis, exactly as in the console: each field shows its default value, its
unit, its help and **where its value comes from** (the signal, `onthesignal.toml` or the
default). Simple expressions are accepted (`2**24`, `1e-3`); advanced parameters are folded.

The result opens in a tab: interactive chart on top (zoom, cursor reading, legend), and under
it the results of this analysis (the navigation of the charts is described in
[Navigating in a chart](#navigating-in-a-chart)):

1. warnings (saturation, gaps, reduced band…);
2. the key figures of the analysis (for `noise_dsp`: RMS and RMS from the PSD integration side
   by side, dynamic range, ENOB);
3. the detail table, in counts and in physical unit (click a value to copy it; *Copy table*
   copies everything for a spreadsheet);
4. tables of the analysis (harmonics of `thd`, Δt of each edge for `delay50`…);
5. the parameters actually used and the traceability (signals, SHA-256, versions).

The charts follow the rules of the console figures: calculation conditions above the spectra,
removed mains lines as red dashed lines, logarithmic frequency axis, fundamental, harmonics
(H2, H3…) and largest spur marked. `dynamic` shows a summary and one sub-tab per figure
(SINAD, SFDR, THD).

The spectrogram is a color map under the time series, both on the same time axis: zooming
one zooms the other. Under the map, the cursor reads the UTC time, the frequency and the
level in dB; the color bar gives the color range (`vmin`, `vmax` of the analysis).

*Export* saves the result (JSON, CSV), the chart as displayed (PNG) or the publication figure of
the reports (matplotlib PNG, SVG, PDF). *Edit parameters and re-run* reopens the form.

### Comparing results

Results of the same analysis can be overlaid, for instance the PSD of three digitizers or the
`lnm` of three channels: Ctrl+click them in the objects panel, then *Compare selected
results*, or right-click a result → *Compare with…*. Each curve takes the color of its signal;
for `lnm` the smoothed PSDs are overlaid and the NLNM drawn once. Under the chart, a table
gives the values of every result side by side (*Copy table* for a spreadsheet, *Export* in
CSV). Results whose figures cannot be overlaid (spectrograms) or with different units are
refused with an explanation; analyses without a chart (`noise`, `frequency`) are compared in
the table only.

## Python terminal

The terminal at the bottom is a **Python terminal connected to the session**: signals are
variables, every onthesignal function is available, and what you do appears at once in the
interface — and conversely.

```text
ots> S1.sensitivity = 40 / 2**24; S1.unit = "V"     # properties updated under the plot
ots> S4 = S1 - S2                                   # S4 appears in the Objects panel
ots> r = noise(S1, remove_mains=True)               # values printed, result tab opened
ots> r["dr"]
ots> for s in (S1, S2):
...      print(s.name, round(noise(s, show=False)["rms"], 3))
ots> /lnm S3                                        # graphical form, then result tab
```

- Tab completes names, attributes (`S1.` → `sensitivity`, `lnm`…) and parameters, from the
  live objects (Jedi). `noise?` or `help(noise)` shows the documentation.
- A block (`for`, `def`) continues on the next line; an empty line runs it.
- Ctrl+C interrupts the running code (a long numpy call stops when it returns); Ctrl+R
  searches the history, shared with the console.
- `plt.plot(...); plt.show()` opens the figure in a tab (*Figures* group). `plot(x, y)` (or
  `plot(y)`, `plot(x, y1, y2, labels=[...], title=...)`) draws numpy arrays in an interactive
  chart instead; `plot(S1, S2)` overlays signals of the session.
- `/` commands work as in the console; a command typed without parameters opens the
  graphical form. `/ai <question>` sends the question to the chat, `/edit_script` and
  `/context` open the editor.

The terminal is not a system shell: it only runs Python and the onthesignal commands.

## Editor

The *Files* view opens text files in the Monaco editor: scripts, `context.md`,
`onthesignal.toml`, reports `.qmd`… Ctrl+S saves (a Python syntax error is underlined and
announced), F5 runs a script of `scripts/` with its form, Shift+Enter runs the selection or the
current `# %%` cell in the terminal. A `.qmd` report has a *Render* button. A file changed on
disk (by the terminal, an acquisition…) is reloaded unless you are editing it.

Help for Python:

- **Completion** (Ctrl+Space, or after a dot) knows the objects of the session: after `S1.`
  the editor proposes `sensitivity`, `lnm`…; inside `noise(S1, ` the signature of `noise` is
  shown with the parameter being typed; hovering a name shows its documentation.
- **ruff** checks the file after a pause of typing: findings are underlined (and listed in
  *Problems* when the file is saved). For a file of `scripts/`, the names of the session
  (`S1`, `noise`) are reported as undefined, since a script receives its signals as
  arguments; other files run in the terminal, where those names exist.
- A `.toml` file is checked when saved; saving `onthesignal.toml` reads the configuration
  again.
- *Ask AI* puts the selection (or the current line, or `# %%` cell) in the chat with the name
  of the file, ready for a question.

## AI chat

The chat on the right drives the assistant described in [AI assistant](ai.qmd):

- each tool call appears as a card (function, arguments, duration, summary) with a link to the
  result it produced;
- actions that need your consent (writing files, running a script, running code) show
  *Allow* / *Deny* in the chat;
- code blocks of the answers can be copied, opened in the editor or run in the terminal (after
  confirmation);
- a message starting with `/` runs the command in the terminal;
- the answer appears as it is generated; the reasoning of the model, when it gives one
  (Qwen3, Claude), is in a folded *Reasoning* block; the header shows the tokens of the last
  request against the context size (`10.2k / 16.4k tokens`);
- `@` attaches objects to a question: type `@` for a list of the signals, results and files of
  the project (`@S1`, `@R3`, `@context.md`). Signals and results are sent as summaries, never
  as samples; text files with their text (20 000 characters at most);
- *Profile* chooses one of the `[[ai.profiles]]` of the configuration; next to it, a green dot
  tells that the model can be used, or a red cross why it cannot (server not reachable, model
  not downloaded, API key missing);
- the conversations are saved in `.onthesignal/chats/` of the project: the history button
  reopens one (the assistant goes on with it) or exports it in Markdown;
- *Allow for this chat* on a confirmation allows that kind of action (running a script…) until
  the next *New chat*; the ↻ button asks the last question again for a new answer;
- the first request to an online profile (Claude, ChatGPT) asks whether the summaries may be
  sent to it; the answer holds until the server stops. Ollama and servers of the local
  network are not asked, as the data stay on your network;
- *Init* runs `/init`, *Context* opens `context.md`; the tune button changes the provider, the
  model, the server URL and the context size for the session; *Stop* interrupts a request,
  even while the answer is being written.

The model receives summaries of the signals and results, never the samples. API keys are read
from the environment of the server only. With Ollama, set the context to at least 16 384
tokens (see `ollama.md` at the root of the repository).

## Reports, scripts and batches

- **Reports.** *Add to report* puts results in the basket of the *Reports* view; *Generate the
  report* writes the Quarto report and renders it (HTML, PDF). Existing reports can be edited,
  rendered again, previewed in a tab and downloaded ([Reports](reports.qmd)).
- **Scripts.** The *Scripts* view creates a script from the template, edits it and runs it with
  its form ([Scripts](scripts.qmd)).
- **Batches.** *New batch…* in the *Scripts* view (or `/batch` in the palette, or right-click
  a folder of the *Files* view → *Batch on this folder…*) runs an analysis or a script on
  every channel of every file matching the patterns (`data/*.mseed`, several separated by
  spaces; files outside the project are refused). The form gives the parameters of the
  analysis, the reading options for files without metadata (unit, sensitivity, text files)
  and the output table (`.csv` or `.json`). A tab follows the batch file by file and shows
  one row per file and channel; a file that cannot be read or analysed is recorded in the
  `error` column and does not stop the batch. *Stop* ends it before the next file; *Export*
  downloads the table; *Global report* writes a Quarto report holding the table.

## Acquisition and real time

Both views choose the streams the same way: server, port, network and station (defaults of
`[seedlink]`), *List streams*, then a filter by pattern (`FH?`, `00.HH?`, `?HZ`) and the
check boxes (*All*, *None*).

- **Acquisition.** *Start* records the chosen streams to miniSEED for the given duration, with
  a live table per channel (samples, last sample, latency, gaps, effective rate); *Stop* ends
  it cleanly. The acquisition belongs to the server: it goes on if the browser is closed, and
  the reloaded page shows its progress again ([Acquisition](acquisition.qmd)).
- **Real time.** *Start* opens the *Real time* dashboard: for each channel, the mean,
  standard deviation and peak-to-peak over the statistics window (in counts, and in the
  physical unit when a sensitivity is given, e.g. `1/6.29e8` m/s per count), the latency and
  the gaps; the trace of the last seconds, one panel per channel; the FFT amplitude and the
  Welch PSD over the spectral window (60 s by default, refreshed every 2 s). The axes follow
  the data until you zoom; a double-click makes them follow again. *Record to miniSEED*
  appends the received records to `<folder>/<channel>.mseed` and can be switched on and off
  while running. One real-time session at a time; it stops with *Stop* or when the server
  stops.

## Configuration

The `[web]` section of the configuration is described in [Configuration](configuration.qmd).
The *Settings* view shows every value with its origin (default, global file, project file,
session); a click on a value changes it for the session (TOML syntax: `8090`, `true`,
`"text"`). Keys that onthesignal does not read are listed. *Edit onthesignal.toml* opens the
project file in the editor; saving it checks it and reads the configuration again.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Solution |
| --- | --- |
| `The web interface needs the [web] dependencies` | `pip install -e ".[web]"` |
| `address already in use` | another server uses the port: `--port 8090`, or stop it |
| The page stays empty or reconnects | the server was stopped or restarted: reload the page |
| The page stays blank in an old browser | NiceGUI 4 needs Chrome or Edge 121 or later, Safari 17.2 or later, or a recent Firefox |
| `Forbidden … (Host or Origin check)` | the address used is not the server's: use `127.0.0.1`, or add the host name to `[web] allowed_hosts` |
| A command of the terminal waits | a form or a confirmation is open in the browser: answer it, or Ctrl+C |
| A channel of the real-time dashboard stays empty | low-rate channels (`LH?`, `VH?`) send one record every few minutes: wait, or choose `HH?`/`BH?` channels |
| A batch reports `outside the project` | the patterns are relative to the project folder; to use another folder, add it to `[web] roots` |
| The chat answers `The assistant is not available` | no model configured: tune button of the chat, or `[ai]` in `onthesignal.toml` |
